author: I Wayan Ariawan
author_headline: Principal Underwriting Analyst at Home Credit Indonesia
comment_text: Spot-on analysis regarding how raw Brier scores (BS) can mask a weak model simply because its predictions hover near the baseline event rate. However, Yates Decomposition (YC) math has a major flaw: its forecast variance and covariance terms can cancel each other out and hide true ranking power. We cannot look at the covariance alone to judge ranking power because its true value is contaminated by the variance. Perhaps a cleaner fix would be this relatively new paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05544. It rearranges the math into 3 simple, strictly positive factors that measure bias (Global Calibration Factor), spread (Variance Mismatch Factor), and ranking (Correlation Deficit Factor) separately. If we want to know which scorecard has the best ranking engine when BS tie, we look at exactly one factor: the Correlation Deficit. Whichever scorecard has the lower number in that specific factor wins. This score will not change just because the scorecard's variance shifts. It automatically exposes Model A's weak spread and rewards Model B's strong ranking power without needing a manual tie-breaker, i.e. trade off between variance and covariance factors in YC.

comment_text: These metrics and plenty more are bread and butter for applied statisticians, so it’s nice to see them getting some air time. It does concern me though how models are being deployed and assessed in this age of “data science” rebranding and development at pace. These methods have been around for decades and are part of a statistician’s core training. But there’s only so much space in a degree programme, and a lot of that depth gets cut to make room for hands-on tooling. The result is that you don’t know what you don’t know. What is the default .fit() actually doing under the hood, and is it appropriate for your use case? Often it isn’t. Not everything should default to Maximum Likelihood Estimation for parameter estimation, or to p = 0.05 as a benchmark. In many applications, a 5% Type I error rate is far from acceptable. It’s not a new problem. I’ve seen it anywhere a point-and-click interface exists for over 20 years, side eye to SPSS. The difference now is scale, speed, and reach. These capabilities are far more accessible, and models are being deployed much faster, often without the depth of statistical insight or oversight that sometimes used to sit around them. Unless we actively upskill data scientists on this, it’s only going to become a bigger issue over time. For me, it’s not about old versus new. It’s recognising that different skillsets matter, and not losing them by focusing on new labels and entry routes without understanding what’s being left behind. It’s about ensuring teams have good coverage of both, either through cross-pollination or cohesive internal training, before that underlying knowledge starts to fade. Because once it does, it’s not just academic. It affects the quality of decisions being made.

comment_text: Just to clarify terminology in this discussion: When we compute “Gini” in SAS, R, or Python for binary classification models, we are computing Somers’ D. Gini = 2 × AUC − 1 In the credit risk literature, this quantity is mathematically identical to the Accuracy Ratio (AR) derived from the CAP curve. So: Somers’ D = Accuracy Ratio (CAP) = 2 × AUC − 1 This equivalence is well established in the literature: - Engelmann, Hayden & Tasche (2003) – Measuring the Discriminative Power of Rating Systems https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2793951 - Basel Committee (2005) – Working Paper No. 14 Studies on the Validation of Internal Rating Systems https://www.bis.org/publ/bcbs_wp14.pdf - Hamerle, Rauhmeier & Rösch (2003) – Uses and Misuses of Measures for Credit Rating Accuracy - Tasche (2006) – Validation of Internal Rating Systems and PD Estimates - Harrell (2015) – Regression Modeling Strategies In other words, the “Somers’ D Gini” reported by statistical software and the “Accuracy Ratio” from the CAP curve are not different metrics , they are the same rank-based discrimination measure expressed through ROC and CAP geometry.

comment_text: Interesting perspective on the Gini coefficient in credit risk. While it is a standard metric, I believe there are a few critical limitations to consider: A. Gini is not always a reliable tool for comparing models across different populations or variable sets. Even a slight shift in the population size or composition can yield different Gini results for the same underlying model logic. B. 'Gini Hacking' - Focusing solely on Gini can lead to the inclusion of variables that are highly correlated with default (close-to-default indicators). While this boosts the score, it often happens at the expense of variables that provide better discrimination among lower-risk segments, which is where the real business value often lies. Precision vs. Recall - We must consider the model's application. Gini essentially represents ranking/recall without accounting for precision. In a business context where rejecting a 'good' customer carries a high cost, relying only on Gini can lead to expensive decision-making errors. So, selecting the right metric should always depend on the specific business constraints and the trade-off between risk and opportunity

comment_text: I completely agree. This misconception appears surprisingly often. ROC-AUC evaluates the model’s ranking ability — the probability that a randomly chosen positive receives a higher score than a randomly chosen negative. Because it is based on relative ranking rather than class counts, it is invariant to class imbalance. What imbalance actually affects are operational metrics such as precision, recall, or business thresholds, not the model’s intrinsic discriminatory power captured by ROC-AUC (or equivalently the Gini coefficient).

comment_text: The translation from Gini to business value is directionally correct, but it holds only in a decision space where risk appetite is discretionary. In regulated balance sheets, that space is truncated by ICAAP, concentration limits, capital scarcity and model governance constraints. Beyond a certain point, incremental Gini does not buy volume or profit it buys permission. Higher discriminatory power matters only insofar as it restores admissibility under binding capital, portfolio concentration or model-risk limits. Once those constraints bind, optimisation on unit economics becomes irrelevant; the question is whether the model outcome is allowed to be acted upon at all. From a Basel perspective, the real economic value of a Gini point is therefore not incremental margin, but its ability to preserve decision authority under Pillar 2 delaying limit breaches, preventing concentration lock-in, and maintaining reversibility when growth would otherwise have to stop.

comment_text: Nice and well-structured solution, Denis 👍 One important credit-risk nuance from a Basel perspective: although PD is trained on a binary default outcome, it is not used as a classification model in practice. PD is primarily a ranking model whose job is to correctly order obligors by risk. The reason is exposure. Two borrowers with the same PD can have very different impact on the portfolio depending on EAD (and LGD). A pure “good vs bad” cutoff ignores that a small number of high-exposure borrowers can dominate capital and loss. For that reason, thresholds should usually be set at the policy layer, based on expected loss or capital impact (PD × EAD × LGD), not optimized directly during training. This also makes it much clearer for stakeholders to answer questions like: “If we reject the riskiest 10%, how much portfolio loss do we actually reduce?” I’d keep the model focused on ranking quality (Gini/AUC + calibration) and derive accept / review / reject bands from exposure-weighted portfolio trade-offs.

comment_text: One more point I really like in your approach is the focus on model monitoring 👍 For credit-risk models, I’d go one step further and be proactive about macro-driven data drift (e.g. inflation, rate environment, cost of living). These factors can silently shift feature distributions and PD calibration over time. In many risk setups, it’s actually safer to exclude highly cyclical macro variables at feature-engineering time and treat them as scenario or stress inputs instead, rather than letting them leak into PD and then correcting only after performance deteriorates. That tends to give more stable ranking over the cycle and clearer governance than waiting for adverse impact to show up years later.

comment_text: This is such a great read — and a reminder that weight of evidence isn’t just a statistical tool, it’s a way of thinking. Turing’s shift from multiplying probabilities to adding evidence changed more than codebreaking; it changed how we reason. Small, imperfect signals can build into overwhelming certainty when combined — the same principle behind every scorecard we use today. It also makes me wonder: additive scoring was born out of pencil-and-paper constraints. In an era where computation is virtually unlimited, are we sticking with it because it’s truly fundamental, or because we haven’t yet imagined the next leap that’s both powerful and explainable? Maybe the future of AI isn’t about prying open black boxes — it’s about returning to that original principle: evidence should accumulate, piece by piece, into understanding. - EB

comment_text: When I was developing large fraud models at HSBC, calibration was absolutely a standard practice. Rebalancing the dataset for the training it OK, but for validation and test, we should ALWAYS use the natural distribution that the model will encounter in the field. But this is not enough, usually there are conflicting and imbalanced objectives that we have to account for, e.g. a risk tolerance of 2% on FN versus an expected 70% gain on TN in case of adjudication models. In this case, building a single model does not give the full picture, even if well calibrated. It's actually better to build several models and plot the Pareto front in the objective space: as a result, the stakeholders have a better view of the tradeoff risk / reward.

author: Denis Burakov

comment_text: Pararawendy, great question and yes, you're right that over/undersampling can distort PD calibration. If possible, it's best to avoid sampling, but if needed, intercept shift (prior correction) can align predicted PDs with the true bad rate (also via logistic regression on scores vs. defaults). You can also apply weights to rescale PDs back to the original distribution. Both methods (prior and weights) are covered in G. King’s paper Logistic Regression in Rare Events Data. author: Andrija Djurovic
author_headline: Risk Advisory
comment_text: Thanks for sharing the post and papers. WoE encoding, along with the binning of numeric risk factors, is probably the most common approach in standard credit risk modeling today. I've noticed also a common belief among practitioners regarding WoE's superiority over other encoding methods. I find this questionable as generalization in practice depends on various factors, such as characteristics of the modeling datasets, alternative encodings, performance metrics, and the binning process. A main weakness practitioners point out with WoE (and other target-based encoders) is the potential for model overfitting, given the use of target values to transform variables. In my opinion, when developing the model, especially within the traditional modeling framework, it's worth testing different encoding methods and making the final decision based on a combination of model performance, business inputs, and operational ease. By the way, a type of encoding not that common in practice but which I find very convenient is nested dummy encoding (aka partitions). It effectively addresses the multivariate binning process combined with the business requirement of different risk profiles between adjacent bins.

author: Jakob Lavröd
author_headline: Senior Quantitative Risk Analyst at Handelsbanken - Quantifying whatever risks tomorrow will bring
comment_text: Good points Andrija Djurovic. There is a bit of a statistical "douple dipping" in that the WoE algorithm trains on data that is then getting used to train the variable link in the second step, essentially using the data twice. As you write, overfitting is a real risk if one is not careful, for example by making sure to adjust the WoE level for the statistical uncertainty (in particular a problem when you get 0 of one type of outcome in a bucket). Another problem is that one can get a strange bias effect in the model. If you reject most bad customers (as one does in credit scoring), your historical dataset on accepted customers (if you have no rejection sampling) will have a correlation between the variables, for example low income customers will have to have other good features, otherwise they would not be let in. Hence the WoE looking at income will underestimate the risk in the lower tail, since all your low income customers will tend to be the "best of the worst"

comment_text: Good point Huy Tran The naïve solution to stabilizing the bins is the Jeffery correction of adding 1/2 to both 0 and 1 outcome, which corresponds to setting a jeffery prior on the probability in each bin. A somewhat more sophisticated solution is to use an hieratical model in which the probability pi of bin i is drawn from a distribution such as the beta distribution. As an added layer, one can also introduce monotonicity, requiring p(i +1 ) >= p(i) (if in order of increasing risk). Such construction means that each bin needs to have enough data to "convince" the model and overwhelm the prior.

author: Denis Burakov
author_headline: Risk Modeling | Data Science on AWS | ML Engineering
comment_text: Thank you for sharing this amazing deck, Adrian Olszewski! I think you have assembled a very rich collection of books on Logistic Regression and the messages are indeed correct, it's never been a classifier, and in the original papers on LR I revisited they also don't mention any classification. But the question in today's reality is into which group should it be put? Regression? Probably not, because it operates with binary targets. To put LR in a separate ("hybrid") category will also not work. Hence, this "classification" of LR is probably here with us to stay. Avoiding the examples of people using 0.5 cut-off to build a confusion matrix for PD models, I can give one example where LR is used as a classification tool: application scoring. When determining a cut-off value of a score (by-product of LR) for approvals, we normally achieve to find the best split point between good and bad distributions. It eventually results in classification: either approved or rejected.

author: Alex Dozortsev
author_headline: Senior Manager | Risk & Capital Management | Risk Advisory Practice at Deloitte Israel
comment_text: An important point regarding the **business context** in which a model is applied: A **Poisson model** is appropriate when the goal is to estimate the **expected number of events** — such as in insurance, where a single policy may result in multiple claims over its lifetime. In contrast, **logistic regression** is typically used in credit risk modeling to estimate the **probability of a single event**, such as default. These models treat risk as binary — default or no default — since, conceptually, there’s "no resurrection": a default is a terminal event. Even if further activity occurs post-default, it’s usually handled by separate models (e.g., LGD or EAD), not by repeating the original probability model. That’s why aligning the model structure with the **underlying business problem** — not just the data — is crucial.

comment_text: Great observations, Dan. It’s been used in credit scoring for decades now, in this very form of log likelihood ratios. comment_text: Denis Burakov Compared with a logistic regression, GBDT introduces the following failure modes: higher estimator variance; stepwise (non-smooth) and potentially non-monotone response; greater sample-size and tuning demands; sharper degradation when data shifts; less straightforward statistical inference (hypothesis tests/intervals); more effort to achieve well-calibrated probabilities; greater hyperparameter sensitivity; inability to extrapolate beyond the training range; ... These drawbacks are most likely to materialize when the data-generating process is close to linear in log-odds. When the true relationship is more complex and the dataset is sufficiently large, GBDT often outperforms, but that is not guaranteed.
